structured_output.hypothesis: If the claim holds, then in sunflower capitula the crossing angles between the two families of contact parastichies are not all 90 degrees. They stay roughly constant across the disc, as in logarithmic spirals, and angles within 5 degrees of 90 degrees are a minority of capitula.
structured_output.pass_criterion: Using per-capitulum measured parastichy crossing angles from at least 30 mature sunflower capitula, with at least 10 measurement points per capitulum, both of the following hold. (a) The median crossing angle per capitulum lies within 5 degrees of 90 degrees in fewer than 30% of capitula. (b) The within-capitulum coefficient of variation of the crossing angle over the mid-disc radial range is below 15% for at least 70% of capitula.
structured_output.fail_criterion: The claim is refuted if either of the following holds. (a) At least 50% of capitula have a median crossing angle within 5 degrees of 90 degrees, so orthogonality is common. (b) The within-capitulum coefficient of variation of the crossing angle exceeds 30% in at least half of capitula, so the intersection is not isogonal.
structured_output.interpretation: 'Isogonal' means a constant crossing angle between the clockwise and anticlockwise parastichy families along their length. 'Orthogonal' means a crossing angle of 90 degrees. 'Infrequent' means a minority of capitula. Thompson's logarithmic-spiral model is only approximate for real discs, which are better described by Fermat or Vogel spiral geometry with a divergence angle near 137.5 degrees. Under that geometry the crossing angle varies with radius and is near 90 degrees only at certain radii. The test therefore uses measured angles from images or coordinates of florets, and sets the tolerance for 'constant' at the thresholds above. The CV in (b) is computed after excluding the central 20% of the radius and the outer rim.
structured_output.no_dataset_reason: I could not identify with certainty any public dataset of per-capitulum sunflower parastichy crossing angles or floret-coordinate data that has a verifiable landing page or DOI. The large portals I know (GBIF, NCBI, Dryad, Zenodo) hold sunflower genomes, occurrence records and phenotyping data, but I could not confirm a specific record that gives floret positions or spiral crossing angles. Naming one from memory would risk a fabricated identifier. The test needs a new image set or a floret-coordinate deposit.
